subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: On 19 November, Presidents Trump and Xi held their third bilateral meeting of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Both sides described the talks as positive and constructive and agreed to draw up an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship” grounded in respect, fairness, and reciprocity. No concrete breakthroughs emerged on trade, rare-earth flows, or the two Americans Washington says are wrongfully detained. Xi reiterated demands on Taiwan; the United States enacted new rules restricting remote access to advanced AI chips in third-country data centers around the same time. Analysts note China has used the high-level engagement to buy time and strengthen its relative position while lagging on prior farm and mineral commitments. A fourth meeting is expected on the sidelines of the G20 in Miami in December.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The conflict that began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on 28 February remains in a tense “neither war nor peace” phase. The United States maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports. On 22–23 November Trump said he is “inclined” to resume strikes after the New Year if no deal is reached and that recent Iranian drone and missile launches (higher than any week in over a year) had been intercepted with no damage. Iranian officials called the blockade an act of aggression and stated Tehran would use “all available means” to counter it; mediators continue efforts. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains suppressed, with reports of tankers hit by mines or projectiles and fires. In Yemen, Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Rabigh refinery (22 November) and continued attacks; Saudi-led forces conducted airstrikes on Houthi positions in Hodeidah, Sanaa, and elsewhere, with conflicting casualty reports. The United States has withdrawn one aircraft carrier from the region.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: The war is in its 1,734th day. Zelenskyy stated that intelligence indicates Russia is preparing new strikes and urged accelerated air-defense deliveries. Recent Russian attacks killed at least 11 near Kyiv (Dymer) and continued intensive drone and missile barrages (hundreds of drones and glide bombs daily). Ukrainian forces have struck Russian naval assets (including a corvette near Benghazi, Libya), oil facilities, and logistics. Front-line fighting remains heavy, particularly around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka, with limited Russian advances in some sectors. Diplomatic signals exist (talks of multi-party meetings), but no breakthrough; reports indicate the Trump administration has pressed for a deal by early 2027. Other developments remain secondary to these three theaters.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China tariff truce originating from the October 2025 Busan agreement has been extended to 10 January 2027. China formally suspended the additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for another two months while retaining a 10% rate and extended related port-fee and certain export-control suspensions. Average U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods remain elevated (Congressional Research Service figure of ~36.5% earlier in 2026 after the Supreme Court invalidated some emergency-power tariffs, which were replaced under other statutes). The Shenzhen summit produced no further tariff relief or truce extension. Rare-earth and critical-mineral flows remain a central sticking point for any longer-term arrangement; China has delivered only a fraction of pre-escalation volumes. Negotiations continue via the bilateral Board of Trade mechanism established earlier in the year.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen continues to trade near multi-decade lows, with USD/JPY around 159 on 23 November and repeatedly testing the 160 level that has previously triggered intervention. Japan has spent approximately ¥27.1 trillion supporting the yen in 2026 (major rounds in April–May and July–August, the latter including the first joint U.S.-Japan operation since 1998). Recent U.S. participation was modest relative to Japanese outlays, reducing the perceived deterrent. Verbal warnings from Finance Minister Katayama remain frequent. The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September (highest since 1995); further hikes are widely expected, but the large interest-rate differential versus the United States persists and supports yen weakness. Broader G10 central-bank trends show divergence: the Fed has tightened, several others (including the ECB in recent meetings) have been more cautious or on hold, and real-rate differentials continue to favor the dollar.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: U.S. headline inflation has recently printed in the mid-3% range (figures around 3.4–3.7% YoY in recent months), with core lower (roughly 2.4–2.6%). Energy and certain AI-related goods remain contributors. The Federal Reserve raised the funds rate to 3.75–4.00% in September; markets price a high probability (~90%+) of another 25 bp hike at the December meeting, with some officials (including Governor Waller) floating the possibility of 50 bp if core fails to cool. The 10-year Treasury yield closed near 4.92% on 23 November. The ECB has kept rates unchanged in its most recent decisions and remains data-dependent. The BOJ is on a gradual hiking path. Overall, sticky inflation and resilient growth keep the bias toward tighter policy in the United States, supporting higher yields and the dollar.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance for 2026 is exceptionally large (combined Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft figures in the $700 billion range). This is crowding out other electronics production and straining the physical supply chain. Tightest bottlenecks include power generation and grid equipment (gas turbines, transformers, grid connections with multi-year lead times), rare-earth magnets and processing (China dominance; export licensing creates price divergences), advanced packaging (CoWoS and equivalents), high-bandwidth memory, and certain optical components (indium phosphide lasers). TSMC concentration in leading-edge logic, ASML in EUV, and a handful of other specialty materials (e.g., build-up film) remain structural. New U.S. rules on remote access to restricted chips and ongoing Chinese leverage over critical minerals amplify concentration risks. Physical constraints (power, minerals, packaging) are currently more binding than pure semiconductor design capacity.

subsections.text: On 19 November, Presidents Trump and Xi held their third bilateral meeting of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Chinese readouts described the talks as “positive and constructive” and stated that the two sides agreed to map out an “action plan for a constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. Xi reiterated that the U.S. should “do the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in the relationship; Chinese statements noted Trump reaffirming the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence. The meeting occurred days after the U.S. Commerce Department issued new rules restricting Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips via overseas data centers and imposing licensing requirements on shipments to certain Southeast Asian countries. China had threatened countermeasures. Analysts note limited concrete progress beyond the existing framework, with the trade truce still set to expire on 10 January 2027. A brief trilateral encounter involving Putin also took place. U.S. panel assessments have warned that leader-level engagement is providing Beijing strategic space while competition in technology, supply chains, and military capabilities continues.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.-Iran confrontation remains active. President Trump stated he is “inclined” to resume strikes after the new year if no acceptable deal is reached, while a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian shipping continues. Iran has claimed interception of U.S. drones (including near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz) and conducted strikes on targets in Bahrain. Shipping incidents persist, with reports of tankers catching fire after hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen’s Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, claiming strikes on the Rabigh oil refinery and other targets; Saudi-led forces have intercepted missiles and drones and conducted airstrikes on Houthi infrastructure in Yemen. Gulf states have condemned Iranian actions. Diplomacy continues at a low level, but both sides maintain readiness for escalation. Risks to energy transit and regional spillover remain elevated.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: The war continues at high intensity. Russia launched large-scale drone and missile barrages (one recent overnight attack involved 186 drones, of which 161 were intercepted). Zelensky reported roughly 2,700 long-range drones, nearly 1,460 glide bombs, and 165 missiles against 20 regions over the prior week, with significant damage to infrastructure, power systems, and civilian sites (including a residential building collapse in the Kyiv region). Ukrainian forces have conducted strikes on Russian vessels (including in Libya) and domestic facilities. Ground advances by Russian forces remain incremental in the east; cumulative personnel loss estimates from Ukrainian sources remain very high. Limited spillover risks to neighboring airspace have been noted in recent days. Other developments include ongoing Houthi-Saudi exchanges and elevated tensions around energy chokepoints.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce remains in place, extended to 10 January 2027. China has suspended an additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods (retaining a 10% rate) and delayed certain port fees and other measures; corresponding U.S. suspensions (including on fentanyl-related tariffs and some Section 301 actions) continue. Discussions under the Board of Trade framework include reciprocal tariff reductions on roughly $60 billion of non-sensitive goods ($30 billion each side), though implementation details are incomplete. China is meeting some agricultural purchase targets (notably soybeans) but lagging on others; rare-earth export flows have partially recovered but remain below pre-escalation levels. The Shenzhen summit produced no new tariff extensions or major trade breakthroughs. The arrangement provides temporary stability, but both sides retain leverage and have signaled willingness to adjust measures if commitments slip. Broader U.S. tariff actions on other partners remain in the background, while technology export controls continue independently of the tariff truce.

subsections.text: The Japanese yen remains under pressure near the 160 level against the dollar, a threshold that has previously triggered intervention. Japan conducted large-scale yen purchases earlier in 2026 (including a record monthly total and limited joint action with the U.S.), and officials have issued repeated verbal warnings of readiness to act against “one-sided” moves. Finance Minister Katayama has signaled that authorities are monitoring closely and prepared for decisive steps. USD/JPY has traded in a roughly 156–160 range in recent sessions, with intervention fears capping upside at times. The Bank of Japan’s policy rate stands at 1.25% (raised in September); markets price a high probability of a further hike (to 1.50%) in December. The Federal Reserve’s target range is 3.75–4.00%, maintaining a wide rate differential that supports dollar strength. Broader central-bank trends show divergence: the Fed is expected to tighten further amid sticky U.S. inflation, the ECB is on hold with possible further hikes, and the BoJ is gradually normalizing from a still-low base. Intervention risk remains the primary near-term stabilizer for the yen, but fundamentals (rate gaps, current-account dynamics) continue to weigh.

subsections.text: Brent crude has traded in the low-to-mid $90s and WTI in the low-to-mid $80s in recent sessions, with both benchmarks posting a third consecutive weekly decline despite intraday bounces on shipping news. Key drivers include gradual recovery of flows through the Strait of Hormuz toward pre-conflict levels, rising Middle East production and alternative-route shipments, and building inventories (U.S. crude stocks rose recently). These supply factors are offsetting the geopolitical risk premium from ongoing Hormuz incidents (mines, tanker fires) and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Overall, the market is balancing a structural supply recovery narrative against persistent chokepoint vulnerability.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: U.S. inflation remains sticky. October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month (core +0.3%), hotter than some expectations and reinforcing concerns that progress toward 2% has stalled, particularly in services and shelter. Markets price a high probability of a December Federal Reserve hike (25 bp base case, with some discussion of a larger move); the current target range is 3.75–4.00%. Governor Waller and others have highlighted upside inflation risks. The 10-year Treasury yield has fluctuated near 5% (recently around 4.9–5.15%), with the curve reflecting both growth and policy expectations; safe-haven flows have occasionally pulled yields lower amid geopolitical headlines. The ECB has held rates (deposit facility around 2.50%) with a data-dependent stance and possible further tightening if energy effects persist. The BoJ is expected to continue gradual normalization. Bond markets are sensitive to the interplay of sticky inflation, energy prices, and geopolitical risk; higher yields raise financing costs across economies and for leveraged AI-related investment.

subsections.title: U.S.-China / Trump-Xi
subsections.text: Presidents Trump and Xi held their third meeting of 2026 on 19 November in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC. Both sides described the talks as positive and constructive and agreed to develop an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. Xi urged the U.S. to “do the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid setbacks; Trump reiterated the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence. Cooperation was discussed on AI (to keep it under human control), fentanyl/narcotics, agriculture, and energy. A subsequent trilateral session including Putin produced a joint nuclear-risk statement but little concrete progress on Ukraine or Iran. Ongoing U.S. chip-export restrictions and China’s critical-minerals leverage remain points of friction despite the diplomatic tone.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli strikes in late February 2026 remains in a stalemate near day 266. Low-level exchanges continue: U.S. strikes on Iranian sites near the Strait of Hormuz (including Qeshm) and Iranian attacks/claims of mines or strikes on tankers and U.S.-linked assets in Bahrain/Kuwait. Iran asserts influence over Hormuz shipping lanes; tanker incidents have run at a high pace in November. Diplomacy via Oman/Qatar has stalled after the June memorandum. Houthis have escalated against Saudi Arabia, striking targets including Riyadh’s financial district (damaging the Public Investment Fund tower) and threatening Red Sea ports (Jeddah) and infrastructure. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted heavy strikes on Houthi positions and warned of further action; fighting in Yemen has intensified with Houthi gains in some southern areas. Trump has indicated he is “not rushing” major new strikes and could wait until after the new year. Senate efforts to constrain the war have failed.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: On the ~1,731st day of the full-scale invasion, Russia launched a major overnight barrage on 19–20 November (following Putin’s meetings in China and his vow of retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge). Ukrainian authorities reported more than 110 missiles (including ~27 ballistic) and 400+ drones; air defenses intercepted the majority. Strikes damaged three bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, critical infrastructure, and other sites; at least eight civilians were killed and dozens injured, with power disruptions ahead of winter. The front line remains largely static, with both sides claiming incremental gains or successful defenses in Donetsk areas. Zelenskyy has described Ukrainian positions as strong. No breakthrough on peace talks emerged from the Shenzhen trilateral. Other notes: Limited spillover (e.g., debris or drones affecting neighboring states) continues to be monitored.
